title: Chapter XIX
content:
The next day opened a new scene at Longbourn. Mr. Collins made his declaration in form. Having resolved to do it without loss of time, as his leave of absence extended only to the following Saturday, and having no feelings of diffidence to make it distressing to himself even at the moment, he set about it in a very orderly manner, with all the observances which he supposed a regular part of the business. On finding Mrs. Bennet, Elizabeth, and one of the younger girls together, soon after breakfast, he addressed the mother in these words, —May I hope, madam, for your interest with your fair daughter Elizabeth, when I solicit for the honour of a private audience with her in the course of this morning?

Before Elizabeth had time for anything but a blush of surprise, Mrs. Bennet instantly answered, —Oh dear! Yes, certainly. I am sure Lizzy will be very happy—I am sure she can have no objection. Come, Kitty, I want you upstairs. And gathering her work together, she was hastening away, when Elizabeth called out, —Dear ma'am, do not go. I beg you will not go. Mr. Collins must excuse me. He can have nothing to say to me that anybody need not hear. I am going away myself. Mrs. Bennet refused to let her escape and insisted that she stay to hear Mr. Collins. Elizabeth would not oppose such an injunction, and, deciding that it would be wisest to get the matter over as soon and as quietly as possible, she sat down again, trying to conceal, by incessant employment, the feelings divided between distress and amusement.

Mrs. Bennet and Kitty having left the room, Mr. Collins began by assuring Elizabeth that her modesty only added to her other perfections. He explained that he already had her mother's permission to address her and that his attentions had been too marked to be mistaken. Almost as soon as he entered the house, he had singled her out as the companion of his future life. Before allowing himself to be carried away by his feelings, however, he thought it advisable to explain his reasons for marrying and for coming to Hertfordshire in search of a wife. First, he believed that every clergyman in comfortable circumstances ought to set an example of matrimony in his parish; secondly, he was convinced marriage would greatly increase his happiness; and thirdly, Lady Catherine de Bourgh, his noble patroness, had twice advised him to marry, even without being asked. She had instructed him to choose a gentlewoman who was active and useful, not highly brought up, but capable of making a small income go a long way, and to bring her to Hunsford, where Lady Catherine would visit her. Mr. Collins considered Lady Catherine's notice and kindness among the advantages he could offer Elizabeth and was certain that her wit and vivacity, tempered by proper respect for Lady Catherine's rank, would please her.

He then explained why his choice had fallen upon Longbourn. Since he was destined to inherit the estate after the death of Elizabeth's father, he had resolved to choose a wife from among Mr. Bennet's daughters, so that the loss to them might be as small as possible when the melancholy event eventually occurred. He then declared the violence of his affection, adding that he was perfectly indifferent to fortune and would make no demand upon Mr. Bennet, since he knew such a demand could not be met. He was aware that Elizabeth's only inheritance would be one thousand pounds in the four per cents., payable only after her mother's death, and solemnly promised never to reproach her with this after their marriage.

Elizabeth found it absolutely necessary to interrupt him. —You are too hasty, sir. You forget that I have made no answer. Let me do it without further loss of time. Accept my thanks for the compliment you are paying me. I am very sensible of the honour of your proposals, but it is impossible for me to do otherwise than decline them.

Mr. Collins replied with a formal gesture that he knew it was customary for young ladies to reject a man's addresses at first, even when they secretly intended to accept him, and that sometimes the refusal was repeated a second or third time. He therefore considered himself by no means discouraged and hoped to lead her to the altar before long. Elizabeth assured him that he was mistaken: she was perfectly serious in refusing him, he could not make her happy, and she was convinced that she was the last woman in the world who could make him happy. She even declared that Lady Catherine, if she knew her, would find her entirely unqualified for the position.

Mr. Collins could not imagine that Lady Catherine would disapprove of her and promised that he would speak of Elizabeth in the highest terms of her modesty, economy, and other amiable qualities. Elizabeth insisted that his praise was unnecessary and begged him to believe what she said. She wished him happiness and wealth and, by refusing him, believed she was doing everything in her power to prevent him from being otherwise. She added that his proposal had satisfied whatever delicacy he might feel regarding her family and that he could inherit Longbourn without self-reproach when the time came. The matter, she declared, should therefore be considered finally settled.

Yet Mr. Collins continued to misunderstand her. He said he hoped that when he next spoke to her on the subject, she would give him a more favourable answer, explaining that he did not accuse her of cruelty because it was the established custom of her sex to reject a man upon his first application. Perhaps, he suggested, she had said enough to encourage his suit while preserving the true delicacy of the female character. Elizabeth, growing warmer, told him that if her words could possibly appear encouraging, she had no idea how she could express her refusal more clearly.

Mr. Collins then explained that he preferred to flatter himself that her refusal was merely a matter of form. His situation in life, his connections with the De Bourgh family, and his relationship to the Bennets were, in his opinion, circumstances greatly in his favour. Moreover, despite Elizabeth's many attractions, there was no certainty that another marriage proposal would ever be made to her, since her fortune was so small that it might undo the effect of her beauty and agreeable qualities. He therefore concluded that she could not be serious and chose to interpret her refusal as an attempt to increase his love through suspense, according to the supposed practice of elegant women.

Elizabeth firmly denied possessing any such elegance. —I do assure you, sir, that I have no pretensions whatever to that kind of elegance which consists in tormenting a respectable man. I would rather be paid the compliment of being believed sincere. I thank you again and again for the honour you have done me in your proposals, but to accept them is absolutely impossible. My feelings in every respect forbid it. Can I speak plainer? Do not consider me now as an elegant female intending to plague you, but as a rational creature speaking the truth from her heart.

Mr. Collins, however, merely called her uniformly charming and declared himself persuaded that, once her excellent parents expressly approved his proposal, it could not fail to be accepted. Elizabeth could make no reply to such deliberate self-deception. She immediately and silently withdrew, determined that if he persisted in treating her repeated refusals as flattering encouragement, she would appeal to her father, whose refusal could be delivered in a manner so decisive that it could not possibly be mistaken for the affectation or coquetry of an elegant female.
